title: My Adult Children Support Me Financially. Can I Collect Social Security as Their Dependent?
summary: After an adult child dies, a parent 62 or older may qualify for benefits if the child covered at least half of their living expenses.
body_markdown:
Even if your adult son or daughter helps pay your bills, you can’t[collect Social Security](https://smartasset.com/retirement/social-security-calculator) on their work record while they’re alive. After their death, you may qualify for parent’s benefits if you’re 62 or older and they covered at least half of your living expenses.1 Here are the general requirements and an example to help calculate how much a parent dependent could get.


## What Social Security Requires From Dependent Parents


Social Security does not pay[benefits for the parents](https://smartasset.com/retirement/son-supported-me-before-dying-how-much-i-could-get-based-on-his-social-security-record) of living workers, even if your[child lists you as a dependent](https://smartasset.com/financial-advisor/tax-implications-of-parent-living-with-you) on their tax return. Once an insured son or daughter dies, your claim must clear several tests on their record. The table below breaks down seven requirements and what the agency looks for each:2


Requirement What Social Security looks for


Child’s work record Your son or daughter earned enough work credits to be fully insured at death


Support timing The support test is measured at the date of death, or at the start of a disability that lasted until death


Proof deadline Evidence of that support is filed within two years, unless you can show good cause for the delay


Relationship You’re a biological parent, an adoptive parent who adopted before your child turned 16 or a stepparent whose marriage to your child’s other parent took place before that age


Marital status You haven’t married since the death, with limited exceptions


Your own record Your retirement benefit isn’t equal to or larger than the parent’s payment


Application You file a claim, since payments don’t start automatically


The support test counts contributions toward everyday costs such as housing, food and medical care. Keeping receipts, bank statements or other records of those payments could make the claim easier to prove. Missing the two-year window might affect eligibility unless an exception applies.3


**** **If an adult child pays part of your bills, a[financial advisor](https://smartasset.com/retirement/find-a-financial-planner?utm_source=smartasset&utm_medium=google_discover_referral&utm_campaign=dp_social_security&utm_content=adultchildrensupportmefinanciallycanicollectsocialsecurityastheirdependent_a) can help you plan for income once that support stops.**


## How to Establish Dependency for Social Security


Social Security generally looks at whether the child regularly provided at least half of the parent’s ordinary living costs. Support can include cash, goods or services covering expenses such as food, housing and routine[medical care](https://smartasset.com/retirement/healthcare-costs-in-retirement) , with the 12 months before the child’s death ordinarily used to evaluate support.


This test has no partial credit, so a parent who falls even slightly short can’t collect on the child’s record. To help determine eligibility, let’s take a look at the example of a parent with $36,000 of support costs during the year before an adult child died:


Expense Annual cost Paid by the child Child’s share


Housing $14,400 $8,400 $8,400 ÷ $14,400 = 58.3%


Food $6,000 $4,000 $4,000 ÷ $6,000 = 66.7%


Utilities $3,600 $2,400 $2,400 ÷ $3,600 = 66.7%


Medical costs $7,200 $3,200 $3,200 ÷ $7,200 = 44.4%


Other support $4,800 $2,000 $2,000 ÷ $4,800 = 41.7%


Total $36,000 $20,000 $20,000 ÷ $36,000 = 55.6%


To pass the support test, the child’s contributions must reach the halfway mark of the parent’s total costs.4 The table’s bottom row shows $36,000 in total costs, and half of that is $18,000. The child contributed $20,000 ($2,000 more than required), so the parent meets the support requirement in this example.


The individual rows matter less than that total. The child covered just 44.4% of medical costs and 41.7% of other support, yet the parent still qualifies because Social Security looks at combined spending rather than each expense.


## Other Social Security Benefits You Could Qualify For


While your adult children are living, you may still collect on your own record or a spouse’s. Here are five main options:


Benefit Based on Earliest age Maximum


[Retirement](https://smartasset.com/retirement/social-security-retirement-benefits) Your record 62 100% at full retirement age, more if delayed to 70


[Spousal](https://smartasset.com/retirement/social-security-spousal-benefits) Current spouse’s record 62 50% of spouse’s full benefit


[Divorced spouse](https://smartasset.com/retirement/social-security-benefits-for-divorced-spouses) Ex-spouse’s record (10+ year marriage) 62 50% of ex-spouse’s full benefit


[Survivor](https://smartasset.com/retirement/things-to-know-about-social-security-survivor-benefits) Late spouse’s record 60 100% of late spouse’s benefit


[SSI](https://smartasset.com/retirement/ssi-benefits) Financial need No minimum age; available at 65 or older based on age, or at any age for qualifying disability or blindness Federal rate, reduced by other income


These benefits do not all follow the same rules. If you qualify on more than one Social Security record, you generally receive the higher applicable benefit rather than two full benefits. SSI is different because it is a needs-based program that can be paid alongside Social Security, although Social Security income can reduce the SSI payment.


**A[financial advisor](https://smartasset.com/retirement/find-a-financial-planner?utm_source=smartasset&utm_medium=google_discover_referral&utm_campaign=dp_social_security&utm_content=adultchildrensupportmefinanciallycanicollectsocialsecurityastheirdependent_a) can help you compare claiming ages if you qualify on more than one record.**
